title: Native Americans in the United States
description: Indigenous peoples of the United States
wiki_lead:
Native Americans (also called Indians, American Indians, First Americans, and Indigenous Americans) are the Indigenous peoples of the United States, particularly of the lower 48 states and Alaska. They may also include any Americans whose origins lie in any of the Indigenous peoples of North or South America. The United States Census Bureau publishes data about "American Indians and Alaska Natives", whom it defines as anyone "having origins in any of the original peoples of North and South America ... and who maintains tribal affiliation or community attachment". The census does not, however, enumerate "Native Americans" as such, noting that the latter term can encompass a broader set of groups, e.g. Native Hawaiians, which it tabulates separately.
The European colonization of the Americas from 1492 resulted in a precipitous decline in the size of the Native American population because of wars, ethnic cleansing, enslavement, and newly introduced diseases, including weaponized diseases and biological warfare by colonizers. Numerous scholars have classified elements of the colonization process as comprising genocide against Native Americans. As part of a policy of settler colonialism, European settlers continued to wage war and perpetrated massacres against Native American peoples, removed them from their ancestral lands, and subjected them to one-sided government treaties and discriminatory government policies. Into the 20th century, these policies focused on forced assimilation.
When the United States was established, Native American tribes were considered semi-independent nations, because they generally lived in communities which were separate from communities of European settler colonizers. The federal government signed treaties at a government-to-government level until the Indian Appropriations Act of 1871 ended recognition of independent Native nations, and started treating them as "domestic dependent nations" subject to applicable federal laws. This law did preserve rights and privileges, including a large degree of tribal sovereignty. For this reason, many Native American reservations are still independent of state law and the actions of tribal citizens on these reservations are subject only to tribal courts and federal law. The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 granted US citizenship to all Native Americans born in the US who had not yet obtained it. This emptied the "Indians not taxed" category established by the United States Constitution, allowed Natives to vote in elections, and extended the Fourteenth Amendment protections granted to people "subject to the jurisdiction" of the United States. However, some states continued to deny Native Americans voting rights for decades. Titles II through VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 comprise the Indian Civil Rights Act, which applies to Native American tribes and makes many but not all of the guarantees of the U.S. Bill of Rights applicable within the tribes.
Since the 1960s, Native American self-determination movements have resulted in positive changes to the lives of many Native Americans, though there are still many contemporary issues faced by them. Today, there are over five million Native Americans in the US, about 80% of whom live outside reservations. As of 2020, the states with the highest percentage of Native Americans are Alaska, Oklahoma, Arizona, California, New Mexico, and Texas.

grok_lead: Native Americans in the United States are the descendants of diverse indigenous populations that inhabited the continent long before European contact, originating from migrations of Paleo-Siberian peoples across the Bering land bridge into North America between approximately 25,000 and 15,000 years ago, as confirmed by genetic analyses of ancient DNA and archaeological evidence from sites like those in eastern Beringia. These groups developed hundreds of distinct societies adapted to varied ecologies, from Arctic hunter-gatherers to agricultural civilizations in the Southwest and Mississippi Valley that engineered irrigation systems, constructed earthen mounds rivaling ancient pyramids in scale, and sustained trade networks spanning continents. European colonization from the 16th century onward triggered a profound demographic catastrophe, with indigenous populations north of Mexico declining from estimates ranging between 2 million and 18 million to fewer than 250,000 by 1900, chiefly due to vulnerability to Eurasian pathogens like smallpox against which they lacked immunity, alongside territorial conflicts and forced migrations such as the Trail of Tears. United States federal policies, including treaty-making followed by frequent abrogation, allotment of communal lands under the Dawes Act, and assimilationist boarding schools, further eroded tribal land bases and cultural continuity, reducing reservation holdings to about 2% of former territories while fostering dependency. Today, 575 federally recognized tribes maintain sovereign governments over reservations totaling 56.2 million acres as of 2026 (per Bureau of Indian Affairs, including the addition of the Lumbee Tribe in late 2025), with approximately 9.7 million Americans identifying as American Indian or Alaska Native alone or in combination in the 2020 Census, reflecting both biological descent and self-identification amid urban migration and intermarriage. Notable contemporary dynamics include economic diversification through gaming enterprises, legal assertions of treaty-guaranteed fishing and hunting rights, and debates over blood quantum requirements for enrollment that influence resource allocation and cultural authenticity. These communities navigate tensions between preserving ancestral practicesâsuch as oral traditions and environmental stewardshipâand participation in the broader economy, where socioeconomic indicators like poverty rates exceeding twice the national average underscore persistent disparities rooted in historical dispossession.
